title: Skills and Learning Outcomes
html:
Overview

By the end of Cyber Hub 1.0 your team will have built, assessed and defended a small business network. This page lists what you will be able to do, and how to say it on a resume.

Learning outcomes

Learning outcomes
Outcome Practiced in CySA+ domain
Safely remove, install and cable rack-mounted servers Cyber Hub 00 None
Segment a network with VLANs, routing between VLANs and DHCP Cyber Hubs 04 and 05 1 Security Operations
Configure a perimeter firewall: interfaces, routes, NAT, port forwarding and least-privilege policies Cyber Hubs 02 and 03 1 Security Operations
Isolate public servers in a DMZ and untrusted devices on a guest network Cyber Hubs 03 and 08 1 Security Operations
Run virtual machines on a hypervisor with shared network storage Cyber Hubs 06 and 07 1 Security Operations
Deploy Linux services on an isolated network from an internal package repository Cyber Hubs 08, 09 and 11 None
Find cleartext credentials in captured traffic Cyber Hub 09 1 Security Operations
Plan and run an authorized vulnerability assessment, and report it Cyber Hubs 11 and 12 2 Vulnerability Management, 4 Reporting and Communication
Fix findings, prove the fixes and document risk in an SSP Cyber Hub 13 2 Vulnerability Management, 4 Reporting and Communication
Explain a physical threat and its defenses to non-technical leadership Cyber Hub 14 3 Incident Response and Management, 4 Reporting and Communication
Decommission equipment so no data or configuration is left behind Cyber Hub 15 None

Note: How this maps to CySA+

The domains come from the CompTIA CySA+ exam (CS0-004). Cyber Hub gives you the most practice in Vulnerability Management and in Reporting and Communication. Security Operations and Incident Response are covered in more depth in the remaining coursework.

Tools you will use

Tools and platforms
Area Tools
Networking Cisco CBS350 switches, Fortinet FortiGate and FortiWiFi (FortiOS)
Servers Proxmox VE, Synology DSM, Ubuntu Server, Raspberry Pi OS, Apache, vsftpd
Security Nmap, Greenbone (OpenVAS), Wireshark
Administration PuTTY, SSH, PowerShell
Documentation Vulnerability Assessment Report, System Security Plan, POA&M

Resume skills

The work in this course maps directly to skills you can list on a resume. Each one starts with an action and names the tools.

Example resume lines

  • ✓Designed and deployed a segmented network with five VLANs, inter-VLAN routing and DHCP on Cisco switching.
  • ✓Configured a Fortinet perimeter firewall with NAT, port forwarding, a DMZ and least-privilege policies.
  • ✓Deployed Linux web and file servers on a Proxmox hypervisor with NFS storage, installed from an internal package repository.
  • ✓Deployed a Greenbone scanner appliance on Proxmox and ran an authorized vulnerability assessment.
  • ✓Remediated findings and wrote a System Security Plan with a POA&M.
  • ✓Briefed leadership on physical attack tools and recommended defenses.

Caution: List only work you can explain

Interviewers will ask about anything on your resume. If a teammate did a task, learn it from them before you list it. Your Team Log records each member's contributions.

Tip: Prepare for interviews

Be ready to answer questions like these in your own words:

  • What is the difference between an access port and a trunk port?
  • Why does a web server belong in a DMZ?
  • How did you check that a scanner finding was real?

title: The Rack
html:
Overview

Your team will work on an APC NetShelter SX 24U rack. Not every device in it is part of this project: the table shows which ones you will use and what each one does.

Note: Your team cables the rack

Your rack starts with every cable unplugged. Working out what connects where is part of the job, and Cyber Hub 15 returns the rack to this state.

Rack Explorer

See every device from the front and back, power the rack on, and follow how traffic moves through it. Click any device for details.

Not loading, or too small? Open the Rack Explorer in a new tab.

Utility drawer contents

title: Rack Schema and VLAN Plan
html:
Overview

Every address, VLAN and port in this project follows one plan. Read it before Cyber Hub 02, and return to it whenever two devices can't reach each other.

Note: How every address is built

Every address is 10.R.VLAN.host.

  • The second number is your rack. The third is the VLAN.
  • For example, rack 3's Data VLAN is VLAN 20, so its subnet is 10.3.20.0/24.

Caution: R is a placeholder, not part of the address

Wherever you see a highlighted R, type your rack number.

  • A device will reject an address that contains a letter, so an error usually means an R was left in place.
  • Your own addresses are in your addressing plan, below.

VLANs and subnets

VLAN plan
VLAN Name Subnet Gateway Hosts
10 Management 10.R.10.0/24 .254 (switch) Proxmox host (.10), scanner VM (.20), admin laptop (.5)
20 Data 10.R.20.0/24 .254 (switch) Team laptops and the vulnerable Pi, by DHCP (.100 to .199)
30 Storage 10.R.30.0/24 .254 (switch) NAS (.10)
40 DMZ 10.R.40.0/24 .1 (firewall) Web server VM (.10), FTP server VM (.11)
100 Transit 10.R.100.0/24 none The link between the firewall (.1) and the core switch (.254)
999 Parking none none Unused ports, shut down
Networks outside the switch
Network Subnet Notes
Uplink 10.R.200.0/24 Your provider, the instructor rack, .1; your firewall's WAN .2
Internet 203.0.113.0/24 Shared by every rack. Lab DNS, time and package repository .10
Internet Wi-Fi 198.51.100.0/24 CyberHub-Internet, broadcast by the instructor rack. Test laptops by DHCP
Guest Wi-Fi 10.R.50.0/24 On the firewall only; firewall .1, guests by DHCP
Out-of-band 192.168.1.0/24 Switch OOB port .254; your laptop .10

Note: Why 203.0.113.x and 198.51.100.x?

Both are ranges set aside for documentation and labs. They look like public addresses but belong to no one, so they can't clash with a real network.

Names your provider hosts
Name Resolves to
www.rackR.lab 10.R.200.2, your WAN address. VIP-HTTP forwards it to the web server
ftp.rackR.lab 10.R.200.2, your WAN address. VIP-FTP forwards it to the FTP server
ns.lab 203.0.113.10, the lab DNS and time server
repo.lab 203.0.113.10, the package repository: http://repo.lab

Note: Why the DMZ has no switch gateway

The DMZ gateway is the firewall, not the switch, so every packet between the DMZ and your internal networks has to pass a firewall policy. If the switch routed the DMZ, that traffic would skip the firewall entirely.

Core switch port map

Core switch port map
Port Connects to Mode VLANs
XG1 Firewall internal port Access 100 Transit
XG2 Firewall DMZ port Access 40 DMZ
XG3 Proxmox host, NIC 1 Trunk 10 untagged; 20 and 40 tagged
XG4 NAS Access 30 Storage
XG5 Admin laptop Access 10 Management
XG6 to XG8 Nothing Access, shut down 999 Parking
XG9 Vulnerable Pi Access 20 Data
XG10 to XG12 Team laptops Access 20 Data
OOB Laptop, for switch management Management port none
Firewall ports
FortiWiFi 60E port Connects to Address
wan1 Rack R uplink jack 10.R.200.2/24
internal Core switch XG1 10.R.100.1/24
dmz Core switch XG2 10.R.40.1/24
Wi-Fi (guest SSID) Guest laptops 10.R.50.1/24

Your addressing plan

The Addressing table in the Report Builder's Diagram tab has a Planned column: this plan, filled in for your rack from the rack number on your Team Log cover. Work from it, not the patterns above, just as real network teams work from their own site's IP address records.

  • Beside each planned address is the one you entered for that device. Anything that differs is marked in amber, so a typo shows up before it costs you an hour.
  • The plan is what the rack should be. Your entries are what you built. A match on paper still needs a test on the rack.

VLAN terms

Think of a VLAN as a separate switch inside the switch. A port's settings decide which of those inner switches it is plugged into.

VLAN terms
Term Definition
Access port Belongs to one VLAN. The device on it doesn't know VLANs exist.
Tag (802.1Q) A label added to each frame that says which VLAN it belongs to.
Trunk port Carries several VLANs on one cable, so frames need tags to tell them apart.
Tagged / untagged Whether frames on that port carry the label.
Native VLAN (PVID) The one VLAN whose frames cross a trunk without a label. A port has only one.
SVI (VLAN interface) The switch's own address inside a VLAN. Devices use it as their gateway.
Inter-VLAN routing The switch passing traffic between its SVIs.

Tip: Three questions for any port

  • What is plugged into the other end?
  • Does that device understand tags? Only switches, hypervisors and firewalls with VLAN interfaces do. If not, it is an access port.
  • Which VLAN should its untagged traffic land in? That is its PVID.

Tip: Tracking down a connection problem

Start with the symptom table on Reference: Troubleshooting, then come back here to check the plan.

title: Lab Access and Laptop Setup
html:
Overview

Set up your laptop before the first lab, and use the class password and naming conventions on every device so anyone on the team can step in.

Class password

In a real organization every device gets its own password. In this lab, every device and operating system uses the same one, so the team and the instructor can always get in:

1PantherGeek

Note: This is an accepted risk

A shared password is a real weakness. In Cyber Hub 13 you list it in your SSP as an accepted risk, with the reason it is acceptable here.

Naming conventions

Device names
Device Name
Core switch rackR-core-sw
Firewall rackR-fw
Proxmox host rackR-pve
Web server VM rackR-web
FTP server VM rackR-ftp
Scanner VM rackR-scan
Vulnerable Pi rackR-vulnpi

Laptop requirements

Before your first lab

  • ✓An Ethernet port, or a USB Ethernet adapter (the drawer has a multiport dongle).
  • ✓PuTTY for console connections (Windows).
  • ✓Wireshark for traffic capture.
  • ✓Nmap for network discovery.
  • ✓Each team has at least one Windows laptop. Several steps are much harder on a Mac.

Reaching the lab and the internet at once

Why the connection breaks

Your rack's DHCP gives Ethernet a default gateway, so Windows sees two ways to the internet. It picks the adapter with the lower interface metric, and on many laptops that is Ethernet, which has no path to the internet. This is why the setup works on some laptops and not on others.

Tip: How the route solves it

A 10.0.0.0/8 route sends lab traffic down Ethernet, because the most specific route always wins. A higher Ethernet metric sends everything else over Wi-Fi.

Set it up

  1. Plug into a Data port on your own rack and confirm your Ethernet adapter has a 10.R.20.x address.
  2. Open PowerShell as Administrator (right-click Start, then Terminal (Admin)).
  3. Read the explanation below, then paste and run all six lines:
Laptop · PowerShell (Administrator)
$lab = Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 | Where-Object IPAddress -like '10.*'
$i = $lab[0].InterfaceIndex
$g = (Get-NetRoute -InterfaceIndex $i -DestinationPrefix 0.0.0.0/0).NextHop
Set-NetIPInterface -InterfaceIndex $i -InterfaceMetric 500
Remove-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 10.0.0.0/8 -Confirm:$false -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
New-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 10.0.0.0/8 -InterfaceIndex $i -NextHop $g -PolicyStore PersistentStore
What each line does
Line Function
1 Finds the address on your laptop that starts with 10.: your lab connection.
2 Saves that adapter's number in $i. This works whatever Windows named the adapter.
3 Reads that adapter's default gateway, the switch address your rack's DHCP gave it, and saves it in $g.
4 Raises that adapter's metric to 500, so Windows sends internet traffic over Wi-Fi instead.
5 Removes any old lab route, such as one from another rack. If there is none, it does nothing.
6 Adds the lab route: everything starting with 10. goes to your rack's gateway. PersistentStore keeps it after you restart.

Tip: When to run it again

The route stays after restarts. Run it again only:

  • after visiting another rack, such as in Cyber Hub 12;
  • if you plug a USB Ethernet adapter into a different USB port. Windows treats a new port as a new adapter, so use the same port every time.

Note: Is this safe to run?

Yes. It's good practice to understand any script before you run it.

  • It only reads and changes your laptop's routing settings.
  • It downloads, installs and sends nothing, and never touches your files or accounts.
  • It needs Administrator rights because routing settings apply to the whole laptop.

Check it

  • Lab: Test-NetConnection 10.R.100.1 ends with PingSucceeded : True.
  • Internet: a website loads in your browser.
  • Back from another rack (after Cyber Hub 12): plug into your own rack and run the six lines again. Line 5 clears the old route for you.

Revert the route

Run these two lines in PowerShell as Administrator to remove the route and put the metric back to the Windows default. They work even with the cable unplugged:

Laptop · PowerShell (Administrator)
Remove-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 10.0.0.0/8 -Confirm:$false -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-NetIPInterface -AddressFamily IPv4 | Set-NetIPInterface -AutomaticMetric Enabled

Caution: Wi-Fi turns off when you plug in the cable?

Some laptops switch Wi-Fi off whenever Ethernet is connected. Look for a setting named "LAN/WLAN switching" in the BIOS, or "Disable upon wired connect" in the Wi-Fi adapter's Advanced properties in Device Manager, and turn it off.

Note: Campus Wi-Fi isn't affected

Campus Wi-Fi gives laptops 172.17.x.x addresses, so the 10.0.0.0/8 route never overlaps with it.

Testing from the internet

Some tests need a laptop outside every rack, where a stranger on the internet would be. The instructor rack broadcasts a Wi-Fi network for this: CyberHub-Internet.

  1. Unplug your laptop's Ethernet cable. While it's plugged in, the lab route sends traffic into your own rack instead.
  2. Join CyberHub-Internet with the class password, and untick Connect automatically. Your laptop gets a 198.51.100.x address.
  3. Check it: nslookup www.rackR.lab returns 10.R.200.2.

Tip: Back at your rack

Rejoin campus Wi-Fi and plug the Ethernet cable back in. The lab route comes back on its own, so there's nothing to run.

Notes for Mac users

You can use a Mac, but plan to borrow a teammate's Windows laptop for console and FTP steps.

macOS differences
Task macOS
Console connection No PuTTY. Use the Terminal command screen /dev/tty.usbserial-[ID] 115200. Some console cables need a driver from their maker.
Internet over Wi-Fi In System Settings, Network, use Set Service Order to drag Wi-Fi above your Ethernet adapter. Drag it back to undo.
Add the lab route sudo route -n add -net 10.0.0.0/8 10.R.20.254, using the gateway for the VLAN you are on from your addressing plan
Remove the lab route sudo route -n delete -net 10.0.0.0/8, or restart
Testing from the internet Unplug Ethernet, then join CyberHub-Internet
FTP login in Cyber Hub 09 macOS no longer includes an FTP command. Use a Windows teammate's laptop.

title: Troubleshooting
html:
Overview

Expect things to break this semester. Finding and fixing problems is a core part of the work, not a sign that something went wrong. This page covers how to approach a problem, how to track it down, when to ask for help, and where AI fits.

The mindset

Note: Problems are part of the job

  • Every engineer misconfigures a device, uses the wrong port or locks themselves out at some point.
  • Employers value people who can find the cause, not people who never run into problems.

Tip: Every result is evidence

  • Every error message and failed ping is a clue that rules something out.
  • Each one you rule out brings you closer to the cause.

Tip: Take a break when you're stuck

Step away for a few minutes, then explain the problem to a teammate from the start. Talking it through often reveals the step you skipped.

The method

  1. Describe it exactly. Not "the internet is broken" but "laptop on XG10 gets no address."
  2. Read the error. Messages like "Destination host unreachable" tell you where to look.
  3. Narrow it down. One device or all of them? Did it ever work? What changed since then?
  4. Check from the bottom up, using the layer table below.
  5. Change one thing at a time, and test after each change, or you won't know what fixed it.
  6. Write it down. Open a troubleshooting ticket in the Team Log: the issue, a work log entry for each hypothesis you test (keep the ones you rule out), the resolution and the verification. The next person solves it faster.
Check layer by layer, from the bottom
Layer Check
1 Physical Link lights, cables seated, the right port on the right device
2 Data link VLAN membership, trunk settings, the MAC address table
3 Network Address and mask, default gateway, routing tables
4 to 7 Application Firewall policies, service status, ports

Tips and tricks

Habits that save time

  • ✓Check the cable first. A cable in the wrong port is one of the most common causes.
  • ✓Ping in both directions. A reply that can't get back fails just like a request that can't get there.
  • ✓Look before you change. Read the current settings before you edit anything.
  • ✓Check your network diagram. A port, VLAN or address that differs between the diagram and the rack is often the fault.
  • ✓Compare with something that works: another port, another laptop, or a neighboring team's settings.
  • ✓Undo your last change. If that fixes it, you have found the cause.
  • ✓Save the configuration. "Worked last week, broken today" is usually an unsaved change.
  • ✓Don't rely on a reboot. A restart can hide the cause until it returns at a worse time.
  • ✓Screenshot the error. You will want the exact wording later, for the Team Log or a ticket.

Common symptoms

Symptoms and likely causes
Symptom Probable cause
Device gets a 169.254.x.x address Port in the wrong VLAN, or that VLAN has no DHCP pool
Has an address but can't ping its own gateway Missing SVI, or a typo in a static address
Pings its own gateway but not other VLANs Wrong default gateway on the device
Proxmox web page stops loading after a trunk change XG3's untagged VLAN is not the Management VLAN
Proxmox host works but a VM can't be reached VM tag missing or wrong, VLAN not tagged on XG3, or the bridge isn't VLAN-aware
Internal VLANs reach each other but not the firewall Switch default route missing, or the firewall has no route back to that subnet
Internal networks can't reach the DMZ No firewall policy from that network to the DMZ
Lab works but the internet doesn't Laptop route setup, on Reference: Lab Access and Laptop Setup
Laptop on CyberHub-Internet reaches nothing Ethernet is still plugged in, so the lab route sends traffic to your own rack. See Testing from the internet, on Reference: Lab Access and Laptop Setup
apt update fails on a VM or the Pi Its DNS server isn't 203.0.113.10, DMZ_to_Repo is missing (DMZ VMs), or its sources still point at Ubuntu's or Raspberry Pi's own servers
A device can't resolve names or keeps the wrong time Its DNS or time server isn't 203.0.113.10, or Upstream_Services doesn't cover its subnet
Proxmox storage is unavailable and VMs won't start The NAS was powered on after the Proxmox host
Worked last week, broken today Configuration wasn't saved to startup

Getting help

Solve problems at the lowest tier you can before moving up.

Escalation tiers
Tier Contact Escalate when
1 Your team Troubleshoot together for 15 minutes
2 Other teams Ask a neighboring team; teams that are ahead are expected to help
3 Instructional aide Hardware problems or unclear instructions
4 Instructor Problems nobody else can solve, or infrastructure failures

Caution: Prepare a ticket for Tier 3 or 4

Write these in the Team Log first. Teams often find the problem while gathering them.

  • The symptom, and what you already checked.
  • For network problems: the VLAN table, port settings, switch addresses, routing table and DHCP bindings.

Using AI

AI tools can help, but only as a last step. Work through the method, the symptom table and your team first. Troubleshooting is the skill this course builds, and an answer you didn't work for will not help you at the checkpoint or in an interview.

Caution: Before you ask AI

You should already be able to answer all of these:

  • What exactly is the symptom, and what does the error say?
  • Which layers have you checked, and what did you find?
  • What changed since it last worked?

Guidelines for using AI

  • ✓Describe your own diagnosis and ask what you might have missed, not just for the fix.
  • ✓Never paste passwords, keys or configurations that contain them.
  • ✓Check every suggestion against your addressing plan and the device before you apply it.
  • ✓Apply one change at a time and test after each, as in the method.
  • ✓Record in the Team Log what you asked, what it suggested and what actually fixed it.

Note: Be ready to explain the fix

Any team member may be asked to explain it at the checkpoint. If you can't explain why a fix works, you haven't finished troubleshooting.

title: Lab Rules and Safety
html:
Overview

These safety and engagement rules apply in every lab. Breaking them can damage equipment, harm someone, or put another team's work at risk.

Lab safety

  • Servers are heavy. Two people slide a server in or out of the rack.
  • Lab devices never connect to campus Wi-Fi. Software comes from your provider's repository.
  • Connect your rack only to its own uplink jack. Never connect it to another rack or the campus network.
  • From CyberHub-Internet, touch only your own rack's WAN address, or your target's during Cyber Hub 12. The instructor rack logs everything that crosses it.
  • Follow the shutdown steps in Reference: Startup and Shutdown at the end of every lab.

Danger: Never connect Hak5 devices

The Hak5 tools may carry live payloads. Never plug one into a laptop, a rack or any other device. Only the instructor runs them, on equipment set aside for demonstrations.

Rules of engagement for Cyber Hub 12

Scanning another team's network is only acceptable within these rules. Both teams agree to them in writing in their Team Logs before any scan starts.

  • Scope: only the target team's Data and DMZ subnets, from its Data port, and its firewall's WAN address, from CyberHub-Internet.
  • Allowed: discovery with Nmap, vulnerability scanning with the assessors' own scanner appliance hosted by the target team, and checking findings by hand without changing anything.
  • Not allowed: changing any setting, logging in with found credentials, denial-of-service tests, or touching any device outside the scope.
  • Timing: only during the agreed lab session, with the target team present.
  • Stop: if anything breaks or looks wrong, stop scanning and tell the target team and the instructor.
  • Offboarding: once the assessors have exported their results, the target team deletes the hosted appliance and its temporary firewall policy.

title: Startup and Shutdown
html:
Overview

How to bring the rack up at the start of a lab and shut it down safely at the end. A clean shutdown protects your work and the equipment.

Powering up

Power on only what the day's lab needs. Working out why something won't turn on is part of the job.

Tip: Start the NAS before Proxmox

Proxmox keeps its VM disks on the NAS. If the host starts first, the storage shows as unavailable and the VMs won't start.

Note: Check the clock

Your firewall, switch and Proxmox host take their time from 203.0.113.10. If a clock is wrong, check that device's time server setting before a lab that relies on logs, such as Cyber Hub 12.

Shutting down

Follow this order at the end of every lab:

  1. Save the configuration on the switch and the firewall.
  2. Log in to the Proxmox web interface and shut down every running VM.
  3. Shut down the Proxmox host from its web interface or with its shutdown command.
  4. Shut down the NAS from DSM (Power, then Shut Down).
  5. Shut down any running Raspberry Pi with sudo shutdown -h now.
  6. Turn off the KVM console, fold it, and slide it into the rack.
  7. Power off the UPS by holding its power button.
  8. Unplug the UPS from the wall outlet.
  9. Return every cable, adapter and USB stick to the Utility Drawer.
  10. Call the instructor to check your rack.

Caution: Follow this order

Turning the UPS off cuts power to everything at once. Anything still running at that point, especially the NAS and Proxmox, can lose data.
